summary: A proposal for an experiment with a Message Switching Protocol (MSP), a system whose job is to switch messages among its ports. Written by Bob Bressler, Dan Murphy and Dave Walden, it gives a specification, message header format, examples and a Telnet-based information operator. It was categorized as experimentation and obsoletes RFC 62.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 333 proposes an experiment with a Message Switching Protocol (MSP) for host-to-host communication. A sender and receiver name ports and a rendezvous host, which matches their requests and forwards the message when both are ready.

subtitle: An experimental proposal to switch messages between ports using SEND, RECEIVE, and rendezvous hosts.

tldr.problem: The authors wanted to explore a host-to-host protocol organized around switching individual messages rather than a stream-oriented design.
tldr.mechanism: A sender issues SEND and a receiver issues RECEIVE, each naming ports and a rendezvous host. The host matches OUT and IN messages and forwards the data and notification to the two endpoints.
tldr.outcome: RFC 333 proposes a limited experiment using links 192 through 195 and says it is not intended to replace the current Host/Host protocol. It obsoletes RFC 62.

today: RFC 333 is an experimental proposal, and the unit metadata lists its status as Unknown and says it obsoletes RFC 62. The RFC states that the experiment is not intended to replace the existing Host/Host protocol.

sections.title: Why Experiment with Message Switching
sections.content:
A Message Switching Protocol (MSP) switches messages among ports. RFC 333 proposes rethinking host-to-host software around message switching rather than what its authors call “stream orientation.” The proposal is explicitly an experiment alongside the existing ARPANET NCPs, not an attempt to supersede the current Host/Host protocol.

The authors report that an earlier message-switched interprocess communication implementation was much smaller than one author's NCP. They propose trying the approach on several hosts and reserve links 192 through 195 for the experiment.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors propose testing a message-based design alongside the current host protocol. They say the experiment is limited and is not meant to replace the existing protocol.

sections.title: Matching SEND and RECEIVE at a Rendezvous Host
sections.content:
A process that wants to send executes SEND; a process that wants to receive executes RECEIVE. Each operation identifies the sending and receiving ports and a rendezvous host. SEND creates an OUT message, possibly with data, and RECEIVE creates an IN message. Each message goes to its named rendezvous host.

The rendezvous host stores the messages in a table. When it finds an OUT and an IN with matching port IDs and rendezvous host, it forwards the OUT and data to the receiver's host and forwards the IN to the sender's host. The two endpoints can choose a rendezvous at the sender, at the receiver, or at an intermediate host.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender's OUT message and receiver's IN message meet at the chosen host. When their port information matches, that host forwards the data to the receiver and a notification to the sender.

sections.title: The MSP Message Header
sections.content:
Each host-to-host message begins with a 144-bit header. It contains the Host-to-IMP leader, destination port ID, message type, source port ID, initiating host's table position, source host, rendezvous host, and a bit count. The header is arranged to avoid fields crossing word boundaries on machines with 16-bit, 32-bit, and 36-bit words, except when a field is larger than the word.

Port IDs are 24 bits. The first 8 bits identify the host that created the port ID; the remaining 16 bits are available for that host's use. An all-zero 24-bit port ID means ANY. Message types 2 and 3 represent SEND/OUT and RECEIVE/IN, while type 4 is FLUSH if used.
sections.plainLanguage: The fixed header identifies the ports, message type, source and rendezvous hosts, and data size. The 24-bit port IDs include the creating host in their first 8 bits.

sections.title: Open Questions and Supporting Services
sections.content:
The memo discusses timeouts, message buffering, acknowledgments, and whether a process should block after SEND or RECEIVE. It leaves blocking behavior implementation-dependent and allows a host to discard an IN or OUT message when it is no longer convenient to hold it. The authors describe FLUSH as a possible negative acknowledgment and note that timeout behavior can create races.

The proposal also describes an information operator that maps symbolic process names to port IDs, and a unique-number process for allocating port numbers. A port-protection process is sketched as a way to check which ports a process may use. These supporting ideas are described as part of the proposal, with some details still needing development.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC leaves several details to implementations, including blocking, buffering, and timeouts. It also sketches services for finding a process's port and checking whether a process may use a port.
